Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are two prominent classes 
of porous materials with exceptional properties for applications in gas storage, catalysis, and drug 
delivery, owing to their high surface areas and tunable structures. This study presents a computational 
analysis of these frameworks using degree-based and neighborhood degree based topological 
indices. We compute a comprehensive set of indices including Sombor variants, Zagreb indices, 
and NDe indices for two distinct structures: a 2D naphthalene-based MOF and a thiophene-based 
covalent triazine framework (COF). The behavior of these indices is graphically analyzed through 3D 
visualizations. Crucially, we validate the chemical relevance of these indices by developing quantitative 
structure-property relationship (QSPR) models for a series of phenethylamine derivatives. Our models 
demonstrate strong statistical correlations between the topological indices and key physicochemical 
properties, particularly molar volume, boiling point, and enthalpy of vaporization. This validation 
confirms the utility of topological indices as robust predictive tools for screening and optimizing MOF/
COF materials, directly linking their molecular graph topology to performance-critical properties.
Keywords  Chemical graph theory, Topological indices, Metal-organic frameworks, Covalent organic 
frameworks, QSPR.
Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are a class of crystalline porous materials composed of periodic arrays of 
metallic nodes connected by organic linkers via coordination bonds. The first known MOF was discovered in 
1959 by Kinoshita et al.1. Research into MOFs has since expanded rapidly, driven by investigations into their 
unique characteristics and synthesis methods. This growth has revealed a wide range of potential applications. A 
key feature of MOFs is their exceptionally high internal surface area, resulting directly from their well-defined 
porous structure. Notably, MOFs exhibit significant potential for gas storage and separation due to their high 
porosity2–6. Additional promising applications include drug delivery7,8, chemical sensing9–11, heterogeneous 
catalysis (particularly gas-phase reactions)12–14, and environmental remediation15–17.
Covalent-organic frameworks (COFs), first discovered by Cote et al. in 200518, are highly ordered organic 
polymers exhibiting permanent porosity. Their porous and highly ordered architecture enables precise thermal 
management properties, including self-heating and temperature control capabilities. Synthesized from organic 
building blocks, COFs possess exceptional structural stability and crystallinity. These materials are functionally 
tunable and synthetically controllable, with key properties including robust covalent bonding and well-defined 
porosity. Compared to inorganic zeolites, COFs demonstrate superior absorptivity, enhanced stability, and greater 
synthetic versatility due to their porous frameworks, extensive surface areas, and purely covalent linkages. The 
large pore structures of COFs further facilitate efficient desorption processes. Numerous applications leverage 
these properties, including energy storage, gas separation, and catalysis19.

The primary objective of this work is to compute both degree-based and neighborhood degree-based 
topological indices including Sombor variants, Zagreb indices, and NDe indices for two advanced frameworks: 
the 2D naphthalene-based metal-organic framework (MOF) and the thiophene-based covalent triazine 
framework (COF). The paper is structured as follows: Section “QSPR analysis and model validation” validates 
the chemical relevance of these indices through quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) modeling 
of phenethylamine derivatives, correlating indices with key physicochemical properties. Section “Topological 
indices computation of 2D Naphthalene framework and thiophene based covalent triazine framework” details 
the computation of these indices for the naphthalene network, including 3D graphical analysis of their behavior. 
Section “Topological aspects of molecular structure of thiophene based covalenttriazine framework” extends 
this analysis to the thiophene-based covalent triazine framework, similarly featuring topological computations 
and 3D visualizations. Finally, Section “Conclusion” concludes the study and discusses implications for material 
design.
QSPR analysis and model validation
The chemical relevance of topological indices, including the Sombor variants and neighborhood degree-based 
indices, has been previously established for simple hydrocarbon systems. For instance, studies on octane isomers 
(acyclic graphs) have demonstrated strong correlations between these indices and physicochemical properties 
like entropy and acentric factor, confirming their utility as molecular descriptors for such structures23,27,28.
However, to validate their applicability for more complex, porous, and modular systems like Metal-Organic 
Frameworks (MOFs) and Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs), a more relevant model system is required. 
For this QSPR study, we employ phenethylamine derivatives (Fig. 1) as the model compounds. This choice is 
strategic and based on the following critical alignments with MOF/COF characteristics:
	1.	 Structural diversity: Phenethylamines possess a consistent core scaffold (the phenethylamine backbone) with 
a variety of substituents (–OH, –OCH3, –NH2, halogens). This creates significant topological heterogeneity 
in their molecular graphs, effectively mimicking the modular nature of MOF/COF construction, where di­
verse organic linkers are connected to metal nodes or covalent sites. The variations in substituents alter the 
vertex degrees and neighborhood degrees, providing a robust testbed for the topological indices computed 
for framework structures.
	2.	 Well-characterized properties: Extensive experimental data is available for key physicochemical properties 
of phenethylamine derivatives (Table 1), including boiling point (BP), molar volume (MV), and enthalpy of 
vaporization (EV). These properties span a wide range, which is essential for building statistically significant 
and reliable QSPR models.
	3.	 Direct relevance to framework performance metrics: Phenethylamine properties particularly molar volume 
(governing gas adsorption capacity) and boiling point/enthalpy of vaporization (reflecting thermal stability) 
directly parallel performance metrics for MOFs/COFs in gas storage and catalysis.
	This strategic alignment allows us to rigorously test whether topological indices initially validated on simpler 
systems can reliably predict material relevant behaviors in complex, highly functionalized structures that 
topologically resemble the building blocks of MOFs and COFs.
	We use linear regression models to estimate the physicochemical properties of Phenethylamine derivatives. The 
physicochemical properties of these structures; Boiling Point (BP), Flash Point (FP), Enthalpy of Vaporiza­

Conclusion
This study computed degree-based and neighborhood degree-based topological indices including Sombor, Zagreb, 
and NDe variants for 2D naphthalene-based MOFs and thiophene-based covalent triazine frameworks. The 3D 
graphical representations revealed consistent growth in index values with increasing structural dimensions (s 
and t), underscoring their sensitivity to framework topology. Crucially, QSPR modeling validated the chemical 
significance of these indices, demonstrating strong correlations with key physicochemical properties:

•	  Boiling point (BP) and enthalpy of vaporization (EV): Neighborhood-degree indices (e.g.,ND4, r2 = 0.445)

applications governed by molecular packing (e.g., gas storage) and thermal stability. Future work will extend
